```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(vellum)
```

vellum now writes enough formats that the choice is a real one. This article is
the capability matrix, and — more usefully — where each format *degrades*.

## Still pictures

```{r}
#| eval: false
render(scene, "figure.png")  # raster
render(scene, "figure.svg")  # vector, web
render(scene, "figure.pdf")  # vector, print
render(scene, "figure.pptx") # editable shapes, slides
```

| | PNG | SVG | PDF | PPTX |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Resolution-independent | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Gradients | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ (native gradient fills) |
| Tiling patterns | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | as a tiled picture fill |
| Hatching (`vl_hatch()`) | ✓ | ✓ (as `<path>`) | ✓ | ✓ (as shapes) |
| Clipping | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | geometry cut in advance |
| Masks, blend modes, blur, shadow | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | as a picture of the region, with a warning |
| Selectable / editable text | ✗ | ✓ (`text = "native"`) | selectable | editable (`text = "native"`) |
| Screen-reader structure | ✗ | ✓ (`role`, `data-*`) | ✓ (tagged) | title and alt text only |
| Faithful without the author's fonts | ✓ | only with `text = "outline"` | ✓ (embedded) | only with `text = "outline"` |

A few rows deserve expansion.

**SVG text is a choice, not a default you can ignore.** `text = "native"` emits
real `<text>` — selectable, searchable, readable by a screen reader — but it
references system fonts, so it is only faithful on a machine that has them.
`text = "outline"` fills the same glyph outlines the raster backend does, so it
is identical everywhere and not selectable. There is no third option yet;
embedding a subset font would give both, and is blocked on tooling
(see `vignette("accessible-output")`).

**PDF embeds its fonts**, which is why it is the format to hand someone when
fidelity matters more than editability.

**PowerPoint is the format for editability.** Paths become freeform shapes,
text becomes text boxes you can retype, and panels become named groups.
DrawingML has no clipping, so geometry that a clip would hide is cut away before
it is written. The same applies to text and fonts as in SVG: `text = "native"`
(the default) is editable and uses whatever fonts the viewer has, and
`text = "outline"` gives glyph outlines that look the same everywhere. A `tex()`
formula, inline math in an `md()` label and haloed text are outlines in either
mode. `vignette("powerpoint")` covers placing scenes on slides.

Geometry far off the page is cut to the page the same way on every backend, so
a mark with an extreme coordinate draws its visible part identically in all
four formats.

Anything a backend cannot honour is reported as a warning at render time rather
than silently dropped, so you do not have to consult this table to find out.

## Animation

```{r}
#| eval: false
vl_render_animation(keyframes, seg, frac, "a.gif", format = "gif")
vl_render_animation(keyframes, seg, frac, "a.png", format = "apng")
vl_render_animation(keyframes, seg, frac, "a.svg", format = "svg")
vl_render_animation(keyframes, seg, frac, "frames/", format = "frames")
```

| | GIF | APNG | animated SVG | frames |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Colour fidelity | 256/frame | lossless | exact (vector) | lossless |
| Resolution-independent | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ |
| Size on line art | medium | large | **small** | n/a |
| Size on dense marks | **medium** | large | very large | n/a |
| Universally viewable | ✓ | ✓ | in a browser | n/a |
| Honours reduced-motion | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | n/a |

The size row is the one that decides it, and it is not a preference — the
animated SVG emits **every frame in full**, so its size grows with scene
complexity times frame count, while a raster format's does not. Measured on a
30-frame scatter animation, gzipped (which is how a browser fetches it):

| marks | animated SVG (gzipped) | GIF |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 20 KB | 61 KB |
| 200 | 80 KB | 296 KB |
| 2000 | **720 KB** | **124 KB** |

So: **line art → SVG, dense marks → GIF or APNG.** An explanatory animation of
a few moving marks is the case animated SVG was worth building for, and there it
wins by a wide margin *and* stays crisp at any size. A 2000-point cloud is 24 MB
uncompressed; vellum warns above 5 MB rather than letting you find out later.

`prefers-reduced-motion` is worth noting as more than a checkbox: a reader who
has asked their system not to animate gets one frame, held, instead of nothing.
That is the last frame when the schedule ends on the final keyframe (the
complete picture of a reveal or a time series), and the first one otherwise.
`vignette("animation")` covers building the keyframes and the schedule.

## Documents and batches

```{r}
#| eval: false
pdf_pages(list_of_scenes, "report.pdf") # one document, many pages
render_all(named_scenes, "figures/")    # many files, across cores
```

`pdf_pages()` writes a document rather than a page: a report's figures, one
facet per page, an animation as a contact sheet. Pages may differ in size, and
each page's tagging survives — every tagged page becomes a top-level figure in
the document's structure tree.

`render_all()` renders independent scenes across cores. It is embarrassingly
parallel — one whole scene per worker, nothing shared — which is exactly why it
exists while tiling a *single* raster across threads does not: that needs
synchronised access to one pixmap, and `PERFORMANCE.md` declines it on those
grounds.

The saving is worth having when the scenes are substantial and there are several
of them (about 3× on four report figures here). For a handful of small figures
the overhead dominates; `workers = 1` gets you the sequential path without
changing the call. Parallelism never changes a pixel — the outputs are
byte-identical either way, and that is asserted in the test suite.

## Formats vellum does not write

Named because "can it?" is a reasonable question with a definite answer.

**EPS / PostScript.** Still demanded by some journals, and a hard blocker for
those who need it. Also a new backend: krilla writes PDF and nothing else, so
this is a PostScript writer from scratch for a shrinking audience.

**JPEG / WebP.** No one has asked. PNG is lossless and the right default for
plots, which are flat colour and hard edges — exactly what JPEG is worst at.
Straightforward to add if a need appears.
